title: Synthetic KV-cache Workload Generator and CI Hooks
summary: Design + prototype scripts to generate reproducible KV-cache saturation patterns for the serving runtime and wire them into perf CI so cache-related regressions are caught early.
content:
Problem statement:
We see intermittent p95 latency spikes under real customer traffic that correlate with KV-cache churn (evictions and small-hit ratios). Existing perf CI focuses on pure throughput and token-level microbenchmarks; there's no deterministic test that reproduces realistic cache pressure patterns.

Goals:
- Provide a portable synthetic workload that can:
  - Simulate a mix of short-prefix heavy requests and long-context completions (the mix matters for KV cache behavior)
  - Control working set size (hot prefix set vs tail requests)
  - Run reproducible sequences to exercise cache eviction & KV sharding logic
  - Emit metrics for hit_ratio, eviction_rate, kvcache_bytes, and per-request latency breakdowns
- Make the generator usable locally and in CI (Buildkite/GHA) with short/long runs
- Integrate flamegraph/trace collection hooks so CI artifacts include stack traces for regression triage

High level approach:
1) Synthetic driver (python async) that hits the runtime via the same API layer as clients (streaming + non-streaming endpoints).
2) Request templates: short_prompt (20-60 tokens), long_prompt (1k-4k tokens simulated via repeated prefix), and context-mix profiles (e.g., 70% short, 25% long, 5% cold).
3) Keying scheme: requests are assigned "session keys" that map to KV cache entries. We provide a hot set (k hot keys) and a tail set. Working set and skew are configurable (zipf alpha).
4) Measurement: gather token-level latency, total request latency, and retrieve server-sent metrics (prometheus endpoints) for kvcache_* counters.
5) Artifact collection: on failures or CI thresholds breach, collect perf traces, flamegraphs, and a short heap map.

Quick usage (local dev):
- Run runtime locally (docker-compose or k8s dev cluster) with kv-cache exposed.
- Start the generator: python3 kv_synth.py --url http://localhost:8080 --concurrency 24 --duration 300 --hot-size 1024 --tail-size 50000 --zipf-alpha 1.2 --mix 0.7,0.25,0.05

Lightweight generator (kv_synth.py skeleton):
"""
# kv_synth.py (abridged)
import asyncio
import random
import time
import aiohttp
from collections import defaultdict

HOT_KEYS = [f"hot_{i}" for i in range(1024)]
TAIL_KEYS = [f"tail_{i}" for i in range(50000)]

async def make_request(session, url, key, prompt_type):
    payload = {"session_key": key, "prompt_type": prompt_type}
    t0 = time.time()
    async with session.post(url + "/v1/generate", json=payload) as resp:
        await resp.text()
    return time.time() - t0

async def worker(queue, url, stats):
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        while True:
            key, prompt_type = await queue.get()
            try:
                lat = await make_request(session, url, key, prompt_type)
                stats["latencies"].append(lat)
            except Exception as e:
                stats["errors"].append(str(e))
            queue.task_done()

async def main(url, concurrency, duration, hot_fraction):
    q = asyncio.Queue()
    stats = defaultdict(list)
    # populate workload
    for _ in range(100000):
        if random.random() < hot_fraction:
            key = random.choice(HOT_KEYS)
            prompt_type = "short"
        else:
            key = random.choice(TAIL_KEYS)
            prompt_type = "long"
        await q.put((key, prompt_type))
    workers = [asyncio.create_task(worker(q, url, stats)) for _ in range(concurrency)]
    await q.join()

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # parse args and run main
    pass
"""

Important metric filters to emit/collect:
- kvcache.hit_count (counter)
- kvcache.miss_count (counter)
- kvcache.evictions_total (counter)
- kvcache.size_bytes (gauge)
- request.latency_ms.p50/p95/p99 (histogram)

CI integration (Buildkite job snippet):
- job: "kvcache-saturation-smoke"
  agent: "linux-small"
  timeout_in_minutes: 30
  steps:
    - label: "start dev stack"
      command: scripts/dev/start_dev_stack.sh --profile=kvcache-ci
    - label: "run kv synthetic for 5m"
      command: |
        scripts/ci/kv_synth_ci.sh --duration 300 --concurrency 48 --hot-size 1024 --tail-size 50000 --collect-flame
    - label: "archive artifacts"
      command: scripts/ci/collect_perf_artifacts.sh kvcache-saturation

CI pass criteria (configurable):
- p95 latency across run < 350ms
- kvcache.evictions_total < 1000 across run
- kvcache.hit_ratio (derived) > 0.92
- no increase in median CPU flamegraph top-3 stacks compared to baseline (see notes on comparison below)

Flamegraph and trace collection:
- Use linux perf to collect cpu stacks on the serving runtime process ID (or container):
  - perf record -F 200 -p $PID -g -- sleep 30
  - perf script | ./FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
  - ./FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl out.folded > kvcache-30s.svg
- For CI we collect two 30s snapshots: one during the cold-start phase and one during steady-state. We store .folded and .svg artifacts.
- Additionally capture user-space mem stats (smaps) and exported Prometheus scrape at start/end.

Artifact storage & baseline comparisons:
- Artifacts are uploaded to S3 with keys: perf/kvcache/<build-id>/{flame-1.svg,flame-2.svg,metrics.json}
- CI includes a simple comparator script (python) that loads latest baseline metrics.json and compares numeric thresholds; for flamegraphs we compare top-N stack weights using a heuristic (normalize weight and compare vector L1 delta). If delta > 0.08 -> flag for manual review.

Runbook for triage (when a CI gate fails):
1) Download artifacts from S3 (link in Buildkite step).
2) Look at metrics.json: check evictions_total and hit_ratio trends.
3) Open flamegraph svg and identify any new dominant stacks vs baseline (e.g., unexpected memcpy-heavy stacks or scheduler waits).
4) If KV eviction rate high, reproduce locally with --tail-size tuned down to make reproduction faster.
5) If CPU stacks point to kernel/syscalls, capture bpftrace for scheduler traces: bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:sched:sched_switch { printf("%s -> %s\n", comm, probe); }'
6) Open INF ticket and tag with diagnostic attachments.

Operational notes + gotchas:
- Don't run with token lengths that are unrealistic (e.g., constant 64k tokens) — server OOM/GC will pollute results. Use repeated prefix-lifting to emulate long contexts without huge memory pressure.
- Prometheus scrape interval should be 5s during CI runs to get decent time resolution; increase scrape to 1s only for very short repro windows.
- When running inside k8s, prefer perf on hostPID-enabled debug pod to get accurate stack info; containerized perf requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN or host capabilities.

Open questions / TODOs:
- [ ] Automate baseline refresh cadence (weekly vs on merge to main) and CI threshold tuning strategy.
- [ ] Add a deterministic seed mode that generates identical request sequences given a seed id (useful for bisecting regressions).
- [ ] Integrate with trace-sampling pipeline to correlate KV-cache misses with request IDs in our tracing (opentelemetry).
- [ ] Evaluate using a Rust-based generator for lower-noise client-side CPU footprint (current python async client is fine but higher variance at high concurrency).

Appendix: quick comparator heuristic (pseudo):
- load baseline.top3 and current.top3 stacks (weight-normalized)
- score = sum(abs(b_i - c_i)) for i in union(top3)
- if score > 0.08 -> label "flame-delta"

Contacts:
- Eleanor Chen (owner) — eleanor@redwood.ai
- Asha Patel (runtime) — asha@redwood.ai
- Diego Martinez (sre) — diego@redwood.ai

Notes to self: keep the script small and readable; tests should fail fast (i.e., short warmup, short steady run) in PRs and a longer nightly job should run the heavy 30m saturation test.
